title: Automated moderation is permitted but responsibility stays with the human moderators, who must provide review
content:
A.2.7.1.2.1.1.2 permits responsible moderators to "use automated tools, including AI and bots, to help fulfill their moderation responsibilities," then fixes the accountability: they "retain responsibility for ensuring that these tools conform to moderation policies and must establish a process through which automated decisions can be reviewed."

The provision is short but it settles two things that automation usually blurs. First, delegating an action to a tool does not delegate responsibility for it — a policy violation committed by a bot is the moderator's violation. Second, an appeal path is mandatory rather than optional, so an automated decision is never final by virtue of being automated.

This matters most against the rest of the moderation regime. The same Article requires charity and a warning before banning, demands a registered reason for every ban, and reserves governance-blocking bans to the Core Facilitator. An unsupervised automated filter satisfies none of those defaults reliably — it does not weigh context, and at scale it silences quickly. Requiring human review is what keeps automation inside the policy rather than in place of it.

The framing generalises past moderation. Elsewhere the Atlas insists that judgment be exercised by an accountable party or escalated to a vote; here the same instinct is applied to machine judgment, with the tool positioned as an instrument of a responsible actor rather than as a decision-maker of its own. What the provision does not specify is the review process's form, timing or standard — that is left to each moderator to establish.
description: AI and bots may assist, yet responsible moderators remain accountable for the tools conforming to policy and must establish a process for reviewing automated decisions.
